multifaceted

/mul-tee-FAS-ih-tid/ - the stress falls on FAS · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Multifaceted means having many different sides or aspects.

Restoring the old mill proved multifaceted work — part carpentry, part hydrology, part fundraising, and part town politics.

Example

Ask the park's head ranger what her job is and she will hand you Tuesday's log: a sunrise search for two lost hikers, a mid-morning grant report, an afternoon spent re-routing a trail around a goshawk nest, and an evening lecture on bears. One position, and a multifaceted one — four professions folded into a single badge.

Multifaceted is more precise than 'varied' because it keeps everything attached to one thing: a facet is one polished face of a single gem, so a multifaceted job, mind, or problem is one object turning many distinct sides toward you. If the pieces do not belong to a whole, they are simply many — call them manifold instead.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

many-sided: Many-sided is the everyday phrasing for a thing with several aspects, and it stops at counting them. Multifaceted adds the gem's discipline: the many sides all belong to one object, distinct faces of a single whole. Many-sided notes the number; multifaceted keeps the sides attached to one thing.

complex: Complex means made of interwoven parts that resist quick understanding — the difficulty lives in the tangling. Multifaceted only says one thing shows many distinct sides; those sides may each be simple. A multifaceted job can be four easy tasks; a complex problem knots its parts together.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

one-dimensional: showing a single aspect and nothing more

simple: plain and easily taken in at a glance

Where it sits · how many distinct aspects it shows — two-sided → layered → multifaceted

two-sided vs. multifaceted: Two-sided grants exactly two aspects — every argument has that much — and stops far short of multifaceted.

layered vs. multifaceted: Layered goes further than two-sided, stacking level on level, but it stops short of multifaceted, which opens onto many distinct sides at once.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — multi

Prefix — multi: many (Latin multus)

Root — facet

Root — facet: a cut face of a gem (French facette, from Latin facies, face)

Suffix — -ed

Suffix — -ed: having

Put it together

Put it together: Multi (many) + facet (a gem's cut face) + -ed (having) = having many cut faces. Jewelers grind a rough stone into dozens of small polished planes so it catches light from every direction; English borrowed the picture whole, and a multifaceted person or problem catches the light on many sides the same way.

Use the root in a new word: facet

Use the root in a new word: facet: The interviewer kept probing another facet of the scandal that the press release had skipped.

Word Choice

neutral / professional

Multifaceted is the boardroom-and-classroom word for one thing with many sides — a role, a crisis, a personality. Keep the gem in mind to separate it from its unit-mates: multifaceted is one stone with many faces, manifold is many varied things, and complex adds that the parts tangle. If you only mean 'complicated,' say that.
